title: Strange botanical: Prism Lungwort After the Cloudburst
tests: Fictional strange botanical; dominant epilithic colony; inflated translucent rain-capture leaves; internal sapphire flowers; crown-vent silver capsules releasing silk-parachute seeds; limestone sinkhole cloud-forest field photography; clear growth stages; no text, poster layout, fantasy glow, fungus, or horror.
prompt:
Create a finished square strange-botanical field photograph titled "Prism Lungwort After the Cloudburst." This is an invented plant species, shown as if documented in a remote limestone sinkhole cloud forest immediately after heavy rain. Make one mature colony dominate the frame at thumbnail scale: dozens of large, paired, translucent leaves rise directly from wet limestone cracks and inflate into ribbed lung-like lantern forms, each leaf 30 to 60 centimeters tall, pale celadon at the base and clear rose-amber toward the crown. The anatomy must remain unmistakably botanical: strong central veins, fine branching venation, pleated leaf ribs, waxy cuticle, water droplets, torn older leaf margins, and dense reddish root mats gripping mineral seams. The inflated leaves capture rain and fog; show pooled water and tiny air bubbles inside their translucent chambers, with soft daylight refracting through them rather than magical self-illumination.

Reveal the reproductive system clearly within the same natural scene. Several mature leaf chambers contain small sapphire-blue flowers suspended on thin green pedicels, visible through the leaf walls. At the crown, narrow vent-like slits have opened around silver-gray seed capsules. A fresh gust sends a concentrated plume of delicate silk-parachute seeds out through these crown vents and across the upper third of the frame, while a few capsules remain split open and others are still closed. Keep the flower, capsule, vent, seed, and leaf relationships physically connected and readable. Younger flat leaves cluster near the roots; mid-stage leaves are half-inflated; old collapsed leaves lie papery and translucent against the stone, showing a believable growth cycle without becoming a diagram.

Photograph from knee height with a weather-sealed full-frame camera and 45 mm macro-capable lens, close enough that the dominant inflated rosette fills two-thirds of the image while the colony continues up the curved sinkhole wall. Use soft overcast daylight filtering through a circular canopy opening, cool mist in the far background, and crisp wet-surface detail in the foreground. Include pitted ivory limestone, calcite veins, moss cushions, tiny ferns, wet leaf litter, trickling rivulets, mineral grit caught in roots, and one ordinary small snail on the rock for scale. Palette: wet limestone ivory, deep moss green, celadon, rose amber, sapphire blue, silver seed husks, and soft gray mist. Rich natural texture, restrained color, believable depth of field, slightly imperfect field framing, subtle sensor grain, and no studio backdrop.

The result must look like an extraordinary but credible botanical discovery whose growth strategy and reproduction are visible at a glance, not a fantasy illustration, alien landscape, carnivorous plant, mutation horror, fungus, glass sculpture, decorative lamps, or product display. No people, tools, labels, captions, poster panels, specimen board, readable text, arrows, borders, watermark, glowing magic, faces, eyes, mouths, blood, gore, or humanoid anatomy.

title: Strange botanical: Tide-Latch Chimneybroom at Low Water
tests: Fictional strange botanical; dense hollow mineral-reinforced chimney stems; hinged glassy tide-latch fan leaves; radial cable-roots in salt-marsh mud; salt-crusted capsules catapulting seeds at rising trickle; golden-hour coastal mudflat field photography; clear growth stages; no text, poster layout, cactus product shot, fungus, or horror.
prompt:
Create a finished square strange-botanical field photograph titled "Tide-Latch Chimneybroom at Low Water." This is an invented plant species, documented on a windy coastal salt-marsh mudflat at late-summer low tide during golden hour. Make one dense mature clump dominate the frame at thumbnail scale: thirty to fifty upright hollow stems rise 40 to 90 centimeters from slick saline mud, each stem a stiff mineral-reinforced chimney with pale bone-tan walls, fine vertical growth rings, thin salt rime, tiny breathing pores, and a few older cracked chimneys leaning outward. The anatomy must remain unmistakably botanical: fibrous green tissue visible inside broken stem mouths, shallow radial cable-roots braided across the mud like guy-wires, muddy holdfast mats, and no animal features.

At each live crown, a hinged fan of glassy succulent leaflets radiates from a flexible green hinge collar. Most fans are fully open and catching low sunlight, each leaflet thick, translucent olive-to-amber, with a central midrib and crystalline salt dust on the margins. A few fans are half-latched into compact umbrellas, and one or two are fully closed into tight wet cones just above the wetter channel edge, making the tide-latch water strategy readable without labels. From several crowns, whip-like reproductive scapes arc outward carrying clusters of gray-white salt-crusted seed capsules. In the near foreground, rising trickle water has just touched a ripe cluster: three capsules have split and are catapulting pale seed flecks on short glistening threads, while neighboring capsules remain sealed and heavily salted. Younger short chimneys with tiny unopened fans cluster at the base; mid-stage stems are thinner with fresher green hinges; one collapsed dead chimney lies half-buried in mud, showing a believable growth cycle inside a natural scene rather than a diagram.

Photograph from a slightly elevated three-quarter field-survey angle with a weather-sealed full-frame camera and 35 mm lens, close enough that the chimney clump fills most of the frame while a shallow tidal channel and distant cordgrass blur behind it. Use warm low-angle golden-hour side light, long soft shadows between stems, specular wet-mud reflections, a light onshore breeze bending a few scapes, and crisp foreground texture with gentle background falloff. Include cracked mud polygons, glassy tide pools, scattered broken shell hash, a single ordinary shore crab claw tip for scale, thin foam lines, and wind-combed cordgrass in the far distance. Palette: wet mud umber, bone-tan chimneys, olive-amber glassy leaflets, salt white, warm gold light, cool channel blue-gray. Rich natural texture, restrained color, believable depth of field, slightly imperfect handheld field framing, subtle sensor grain, and no studio backdrop.

The result must look like an extraordinary but credible botanical discovery whose hollow-stem support strategy, hinged tide-latch fans, and water-triggered seed catapults are visible at a glance, not a fantasy illustration, alien landscape, cactus product shot, desert succulent cliche, carnivorous plant, mutation horror, fungus, glass sculpture, or decorative reed arrangement.
